result: the file's own note says asking whether a value changed anything cannot be answered in general. It can be answered here, because the README made this one load-bearing

decision: Tablet is clean, so the width I had not looked at closes rather than opens
why: I named 768 as unmeasured last turn and it is where the multi-column grids first engage, so it was the likely place for a break
evidence: all nine pages scroll sideways nowhere at 768, and the same fifteen small controls on the forms page still keep 24px between centres. Nothing there needs a change
result: the two widths I can emulate are both clean with the content these pages carry, which is a narrower claim than the pages being right at every width

decision: A menu can be wider than the screen it is on, and nothing stopped it
why: the dialog, the popover and the tooltip each clamp to min(92vw, …). The menu stated a minimum and no maximum, and its items do not wrap, so its width is whatever its longest label wants
evidence: one long label at 375px took the popup to 646 and the page scrolled 311 sideways. Base UI publishes --available-width for this and the popup was ignoring it; adding it brings the popup to 354 with its right edge on the viewport
result: the select and the combobox draw over the menu's popup, so the one class covers all three. What overflow is left is the library's own positioner at 385 wide, not the kit's popup, and hacking around that from here would be the wrong place to fix it

decision: I gave the menu item an ellipsis that could never appear
why: a label passed as a child is an anonymous flex item, so text-overflow on the row has no element to act on. It clipped and pushed the shortcut out of sight while reading in the source like truncation
evidence: backed it out and put overflow-hidden on the popup instead, which is honest about what happens: a label too long for the room is cut at the popup's edge rather than painted outside its border
result: the fix that looks like it handles a case and does not is worse than the case, because the next reader stops looking

decision: Height was the same question and three surfaces failed it
why: only the select and the combobox named a ceiling. The menu, the popover and the dialog named none, and a popup taller than the window has nowhere to put what does not fit
evidence: at 375 by 500 the menu reached 506 against 489 of room and clipped the rest with no scroll, the popover reached 545 and painted off the screen, and the dialog reached 752 in a 500 tall window with its top at minus 126 — its title and both of its actions out of reach
result: the two positioned popups read --available-height, which is what the select was already doing. The dialog has no positioner, so it takes 92vh, the mate of the 92vw it already had. Menu 474, popover 474, dialog 451 with its top back at 25, all three scrolling

decision: I said the height cap stopped Base UI flipping a popup, and it does not
why: I appended content to an open popover, saw it stay on the cramped side, removed the cap and watched it flip — and read that as the cap being the cause
evidence: the flip only ran because removing the cap went with a resize event that forced a reposition. Opened fresh with nothing below the trigger and 252 above, the menu flips to the top and draws its full 143 with the cap in place
result: two things changed between the two readings and I named the wrong one. A test that moves one thing is the only test that says which thing moved

decision: A surface that caps its height and cannot scroll is a surface that hides things
why: the cap is half the fix. Without somewhere for the overflow to go it turns an overflowing popup into a truncated one, which looks tidier and is worse
evidence: the rule asks each floating surface for a width ceiling, a height ceiling, and a scroll to go with the height. Dropping the popover's cap fails it by name
result: the tooltip is capped by nothing on purpose and is named in the rule rather than passed over: it closes when the pointer leaves, so a scrollbar on one is a control nobody could reach

decision: I capped the dialog by hand a commit before reading what the library gives
why: I went to the height question with a fix in mind and wrote 92vh, which cured the symptom. Then I opened the component's own page to settle a footer question and found a part the kit never mounted
evidence: Base UI ships Dialog.Viewport, a container for the popup that can be made scrollable, and documents two arrangements around it. The kit was placing the popup by hand with fixed and two translates, which is the library's job restated in the kit's words
result: the right symptom does not make it the right mechanism. Reading the page for the component I was editing would have cost one call before the commit rather than after it

decision: The dialog sits in the viewport Base UI gives it, and the viewport is what scrolls
why: a hand-placed popup with a 92vh cap scrolls inside itself, which reads as a box with a bar in it. The library's first arrangement lets the dialog keep its shape and move through the window instead
evidence: took the outside arrangement: the viewport is fixed inset-0 with a grid that centres and its own padding, and the popup is w-full max-w-[440px] with no placement of its own. Measured at 1280 by 800 the dialog is 431 by 134 and centred on both axes, exactly what it was
result: at 375 by 500 a tall dialog keeps its full 752 with its top at 24 rather than minus 126, the viewport scrolls and holds its padding at both ends, and the footer is wholly on screen when you reach it. Dismissing by clicking outside still works, and the buttons inside still take a click

decision: The footer arrives at the end of the dialog rather than sitting on a bar
why: the question was whether a long dialog should pin its actions while its body scrolls, which is the second arrangement Base UI documents
evidence: that one needs a scroll region around a body, so a consumer would have to say which children are the body. The first arrangement makes the actions reachable with no change a consumer can see, and it is the one the library lists first
result: so no sticky footer. If a dialog ever grows long enough that the actions need to be in view throughout, that is the moment to introduce the body region, and not before

decision: The dialog was the only component restating a part its library already ships
why: finding one made me expect more, so I listed what each Base UI component ships against what the kit mounts rather than guessing which was next
evidence: the parts the kit leaves out are extras: submenus, chip inputs, scroll arrows, an arrow. The semantics hold without them, checked in the page — the select's popup carries the listbox role itself with every option inside it, the combobox sets aria-controls and moves aria-activedescendant onto a real option, and its highlight draws the accent fill it inherits from the menu
result: a survey that closes is a result. The kit mounts eight parts of the dialog, six of the tooltip, and what it skips elsewhere it skips because the kit has no submenus and no chips

decision: The combobox already announces an empty result, so Base UI's Status part would add nothing
why: Status exists for a list that loads on its own, and I wanted to know whether the kit needed it before reaching for it
evidence: filtered to nothing in the page: the empty part renders its own words and carries aria-live polite itself, so a reader hears them without another region around it
result: the part a library ships is worth reading before it is worth mounting. This one is for asynchronous lists and the kit filters in place

decision: A popup that places itself is standing in for a part nobody mounted
why: the dialog centred itself with fixed and two translates and looked correct, which is why it survived. Every one of these has a library part that decides where it goes — a positioner for the five that hang off a trigger, a viewport for the one that centres
evidence: the rule asks each of the six popups whether it positions itself. Putting the dialog's fixed and translates back fails it by name
result: it catches the shape of the mistake rather than the one instance of it, which is the only version worth keeping

decision: The combobox page asks for a labelled field and every control on every page has a name
why: I had read the dialog's page in full and compared the other five by their parts, so a page could still hold guidance the parts do not show
evidence: swept nine pages for a control with no accessible name and found none out of 43 on the forms page alone, with a planted nameless button caught to prove the sweep was live. The combobox field is named go to through aria-labelledby, and all five form controls already carry the note that they take their name from a Field
result: two clean surveys in a row is a result and not a reason to stop looking. The one place a name comes from a component rather than a page is the tooltip trigger, which is already covered

decision: Four containers painted a ground and left the seat behind them at the page
why: the seat rule can only weigh a seat some component wrote down, so a container that paints and never names is invisible to it — the toolbar tray, and the dialog, menu and popover popups
evidence: measured on a focused toolbar button: the ring offset painted rgb(8, 9, 10), the page ground, on a tray whose own fill is rgb(14, 15, 17). A two pixel band of the wrong black between the button and its ring
result: all four now restate the surface they paint, the way every Surface tone already did. The same button now offsets against rgb(14, 15, 17), and the 3:1 rule still clears with the surface among its seats

decision: A container that brings in a control which rings itself has to name the ground it paints
why: the fix is worth nothing if the fifth container arrives without it, and the existing rule cannot see one — it reads only what was written down
evidence: the rule asks each file that paints a ground whether it also composes the button or the input, and if so whether it names a seat. Taking the seat off the toolbar fails it by name
result: the icon tile paints and rings the same element, so its ring belongs to what the tile sits on rather than to its own fill and it stays quiet. The tooltip is named rather than passed over: its popup paints and it composes the button, but that button is its trigger and sits outside the popup

decision: Every ringed control on every page seats on the ground actually behind it
why: I fixed four containers by reading files, which says nothing about what a control ends up with once the page nests one surface inside another
evidence: walked from each ringed control up to the nearest painted ancestor on all nine pages and compared it against the seat the control computes. One class of mismatch came back and it was my own measurement: the receipt's action reads a seat of #faf9f5 while the walk found the page ground
result: a gradient sets no background colour, so the walk went straight past the paper. The receipt's parent paints a gradient whose first stop is rgb(250, 249, 245), which is the seat, and it rings with the paper ink rather than the accent — right on both counts

decision: The seat the paper names has to be the stop the paper starts at
why: paper is the one ground painted as a gradient, so neither the file rule nor a walk up the page can see it. Two declarations hold it together by hand and nothing said they had to agree
evidence: a gradient starting at another colour would leave the receipt offsetting against a colour the paper no longer has anywhere. Moving the first stop fails the new rule and the older paper rule at once
result: they catch different drifts. The older one pins the stop to a literal, so changing both the stop and the literal would pass it; this one ties the seat to whatever the gradient starts with

decision: The ring on paper clears at both ends of the sheet, and only one end was ever read
why: the ring rule weighs the ring against the seat, and the seat is the top of the sheet. The receipt's action is the last thing on the paper, so the outer edge of its ring lands on whatever the gradient has reached by then
evidence: computed from the declaration: the paper ink reaches 13.48 against the top stop and 12.03 against the foot, both far above the three a non-text mark is asked for. The labels clear 5.76 and 5.14, above the four and a half for text at either end
result: no defect, and now a rule rather than an assumption. Darkening only the foot fails it, which is the edit the old rule could not see

decision: The paper hairline is decoration, and now something says why rather than my saying so twice
why: I exempted it from the three to one twice on the word decorative, which is a judgement about what a mark carries and not a measurement. An exemption nobody wrote down is an exemption nobody can check
evidence: two things make it true. The rule draws as a plain div with no role, so it is announced to nobody, and the total above it is told apart by weight and size — the variant sets a heavier name and a larger amount, so a reader who never sees the line still knows which figure is the total
result: the exemption is now tied to both. Emptying the total variant fails it, which is exactly the edit that would make the line the only divider and turn a fair exemption into a defect

decision: A printed rule is not a separator, so the receipt keeps drawing its own
why: the receipt draws a divider by hand while the kit exports one over Base UI, which is the shape that caught the dialog out, so it was worth asking whether this was the same mistake
evidence: it is not. The kit's separator carries role separator and a solid line token; the paper rule has no role on purpose and paints a repeating gradient in paper ink. Folding it in would add the role I had just pinned it as lacking and override the only class the base contributes
result: reuse that fights the thing being reused is not reuse. The two look alike in the source and are different objects: one divides, the other is printed on the paper

decision: Three parts draw a line on a surface and one of them drew the wrong one
why: the toolbar painted --pk-line, the token a tray takes for its own outer edge against the page. The kit's separator and the menu's both paint --pk-line-inner, which is the one named for a line inside a surface
evidence: two of three agreed and the naming backs them, and nothing anywhere stated an intent for a toolbar to differ, so it was drift and not a decision. Confirmed on the element: the divider now paints rgb(22, 24, 26) like the kit's, while the tray's border stays rgb(31, 33, 36)
result: the rule holds all three to one token so a fourth cannot wander. Putting the toolbar back on the border token fails it by name. The receipt's rule is left out and said to be left out, since it is decoration with a gradient rather than a line token

decision: A sparkline shows a figure at its head that nobody was told
why: the drop line reaches only 2.34 against a card, so I went to check whether it needed a ratio. It does not — the plot is aria-hidden and the root is one img with one name, which makes every mark inside it decoration by construction
evidence: the same structure hides the caption. One page drew 20ms at the head under the name p95 latency over 96 hours, so a reader who could not see the chart got the window and never the figure. The name now ends with the latest reading, taken from the same constant the badge draws
result: a rule follows it: a caption drawn and not said in the name is reported, and a page that passes no label at all is fine, because the component's own name already ends with the latest reading

decision: My own edit stopped a rule from checking a chart, and its floor caught it
why: the series-length rule read label as a double-quoted string. Writing the latency label as a template so it could carry the figure dropped that chart out of the count, from four to three
evidence: the floor of more than three failed on the next full run, which is the whole reason it is there. Reading only one of the two ways a name is written is a hole that looks like a pass
result: the rule reads both forms now rather than the floor being lowered. A count that quietly falls is worth more than a count that is allowed to

decision: I nearly added a latest reading to every chart name, and only one needed it
why: the caption fix made me want the same everywhere, so I went to add it to the commits and frame labels too
evidence: only what sits inside role img is dropped. The label and meta beside each chart are ordinary text and already read, and the frame card states its latest in a meta — so adding it to that name would say the number twice
result: the rule I already wrote is the right shape and the wider one would have been noise. What a component mutes is the question, not what a component draws

decision: A breakdown drew its shares and named itself three words
why: the legend is muted on purpose, on the grounds that the bar's own name lists every part and its share. That is true of the name the component builds and false of one a page passes instead
evidence: two cards passed language split. A reader saw TypeScript 84%, WGSL 9%, CSS 7% and heard three words. Both now read language split, followed by the shares, taken from the kit's own breakdownLabel
result: found by walking the accessibility tree of nine pages rather than by reading files: computed what survives aria-hidden and role img, then asked which drawn words never appear in it

decision: The function the docs tell a consumer to call did not reach the entry
why: writing the fix into the prop's own documentation made the gap obvious — breakdownLabel is exported from its module and not from the package, so a consumer could not do what the docs asked
evidence: eleven helpers are in that position and only activityLevel reaches the entry. Some are internals a consumer has no use for; this one the documentation now depends on, so it is exported and the rest are left alone
result: the entry rules check what the entry claims against what arrives. Nothing checks what a component offers against what the entry passes on, which is where this sat

decision: The activity grid says more than I claimed, and the arrows say the rest
why: I said its name gave a window and nothing about the distribution, which was my own output truncated at forty characters rather than what the grid does
evidence: the name ends with the total — 182 days, a date range, 660 in total. The grid takes focus, advertises its arrow keys, and walking a day updates a polite region that reads three contributions, Thu Sep 10. A reader gets the summary and then every cell
result: I called a gap from a string I had cut short myself. The axis months stay muted and that is right, because a reader walking the grid is given each date with its count

decision: Seven sentences on one page spoke through a live region
why: the kit had one mono role and it announces. A page marking a term in prose reached for the only thing that looked right, so a reader met seven regions that say Field and never change again
evidence: Readout sets role status and aria-live polite, which is correct for a figure that changes in place. Six of the seven text styles have a plain component and readout was the only one that did not, so the missing half of the pattern is what the pages were substituting for
result: Code is that half: the same mono, a code element, no voice. The forms page has zero live regions now, and the foundations table shows the pair so the difference between them is visible rather than buried

decision: Two roles that look identical and only one of them speaks
why: the substitution is invisible on the page — same font, same size, same ink — so nothing but a rule will catch it coming back
evidence: the rule reads inside each Prose block for a Readout. A readout outside a sentence is a readout doing its job and is left alone; putting one term back inside a sentence fails it by name
result: a difference nobody can see is a difference that needs writing down. The component says it too, on both roles, so a consumer choosing between them is told which one talks

decision: The slider's silent output is right, and its hidden input is the control
why: five outputs on the controls page carry aria-live off, which looked like a value nobody is told about as it is dragged
evidence: the real control is a native range input, named intensity, min nought max a hundred, and a screen reader reads it as it moves. Silencing the output stops the same figure being said twice. The input is clipped to nothing and parked, and the visible slider draws its ring through has-focus-visible, which I watched land
result: I dismissed those thirteen by thirteen boxes once as hidden inputs, which was the right call for the wrong reason. They are not decoration, they are the control, and what a pointer aims at is the 208 by 41 slider around them

decision: An exception in a variant table names a variant, or it names nothing at all
why: the table reads a component's own variants so it cannot fall behind, except for the one list written by hand. A name that matches nothing is silent both ways: every row still draws, and the row meant to go stays and describes state as a prop
evidence: two pages leave one out each. Renaming either variant fails the new rule by the name of the typo, rather than by the symptom further down the page
result: it overlaps a rule already there and does not replace it. That one reads the consequence and fires only when the key it finds is one it knows to be state; this one reads the cause and fires for any name, so a renamed variant is reported as the typo it is

decision: A table's heading is the last thing on it nobody had tied to its rows
why: forty-six tables carry one and every one is typed by hand, so a section copied and half-edited would print one component's name over another's rows and read as perfectly correct
evidence: a props table takes its type, so the heading is that type's name and the two have to agree exactly. Putting the separator's variants under the word toolbar fails the rule by both names
result: a variants object may dress more than one part, so its heading has to begin with the owner's name rather than equal it. That is what naming a part looks like, and it needs no list of exceptions to allow it

decision: Two headings that looked wrong were the only two that could not be
why: my first pass compared each heading with its variants object and reported the terminal's command and the receipt's line
evidence: both are parts drawn by their parent's variants, which a note in another file already said. A rule built on equality would have called the two correct tables defects and taught the next reader to loosen it
result: the invariant is that a heading names the component or a part of it. Starting with the owner's name says exactly that, so the two pass on the same reading that catches a wrong name

decision: Thirteen of the seventeen unions a page describes cannot be weighed here
why: a row states values and a fallback, which is a union written by hand beside a table that generates itself, so it is the same shape as the two I had just tied down
evidence: those thirteen describe a Base UI type — a side, an align, a modal, an axis — and none of the seven components carrying them declares a single variant of its own. A type is gone by the time a test runs, so there is nothing to read
result: saying which four can be checked is worth more than a rule that quietly covers a quarter of its subject and reads as though it covers all of it

decision: The four rows that can be weighed are the two defaults I introduced
why: the toolbar's button and the popover's trigger draw over the kit's button, so their tone and size are a variant this package owns and a fallback this package sets
evidence: the first cut compared the union and passed a changed default, because dropping ghost and adding soft still adds up to the same four tones. The fallback has to be read as well, and from the part's own signature
result: a part settles a default in its signature or leaves the button's standing — both name a tone and neither names a size — so the fallback is read from the signature first and the variants object second. Changing the toolbar button's default tone now fails by name

decision: The thirteen unions a test cannot read are ones the compiler can
why: I had written the limit down as though it were the end of it. The types are gone when a test runs and present when the package is checked, and the check runs over these pages already
evidence: the row type is one row per key now, so values is that key's own type rather than any string. Writing a side of righte is a type error naming the row, the prop and the component. Two rules read the same rows from two sides — one at runtime for what this package owns, one at build time for what Base UI does
result: the same table wrote the limit and the answer. A limit is worth recording and worth returning to, and I returned to it one turn later rather than leaving it as a line in a log

decision: A fallback stays a plain string, because a default is not always a literal
why: typing it alongside values broke exactly two rows out of twenty-eight: the bars fall back to the largest value and the grid's thresholds to 1 · 3 · 6 · 10
evidence: both are true and both are the clearest way to say those defaults — one is computed from the data and the other is an array rendered for a reader. Neither is a value the prop accepts
result: moving them into notes would have typed the field and cost two rows the accent that marks a default, which is the signal a reader uses to tell a default from a value. The drift-prone half is the value list, and that half is now checked

decision: The exception list is keyed to the object it excepts from
why: the props table had just been keyed to its own type, and the variants table had the same shape of hand-written input sitting beside a generated one
evidence: Api is generic over what it reads now, so except takes that object's own variant keys. Writing ticked where the radio has checked is a type error that names the alternatives: ticked is not assignable to checked or layout
result: tailwind-variants keeps the literal keys on the object it returns, so the constraint costs nothing at the call site and the pages did not change

decision: The rule I wrote one turn ago for that is gone, not kept beside the type
why: it read the same tags for the same mistake and reported it later, at a test run rather than at the tag, without naming what the valid keys were
evidence: two owners for one invariant is the thing the architecture rules warn about, and the weaker owner is the one to remove. Its note stays where it stood, saying what replaced it
result: the state rule further down is a different question and stays. It asks whether a state variant is being shown as a prop at all, not whether the name used to leave it out exists

decision: The heading cannot be typed, so the rule for it is the only owner there
why: I checked whether name could be keyed the way except now is
evidence: it cannot. A heading is prose — toggle group, terminal command — and no type carries it. There is nothing to derive it from, so the runtime rule remains the only thing tying a heading to its rows
result: the two hand-written inputs to a table end in different places for a reason worth stating: one had a type to be keyed to and one never will

decision: A section's heading and a table's name are not two statements of one thing
why: I was going to tie each table to the Kind above it, on the reading that a page states the same name twice
evidence: five sections out of fifteen say otherwise. The switch section documents the field, and marks, rows, print and readouts in a card are categories holding several components. A Kind names a section and a name names a component
result: the rule would have codified a premise the page disproves in a third of its sections. Measuring the pairs first is what stopped it, the same as the heading rule two turns ago

decision: Three house rules I went to check were already owned, and one had already found the miss I would have
why: no raw class string appears in any component or page, and the rule for it reads both — its own note records that an earlier version read only src and checked half the surface while looking complete
evidence: the ten composites the design doc names are all still exported, and the text block it reproduces still matches the file. Nothing there had gone stale under this session's changes
result: a survey that finds its subject already covered is worth the time it takes to be sure. What it left was one thing the doc did not say, rather than anything it said wrongly

decision: What the typed values catch, tried rather than reasoned about
why: I had left this as unmeasured for a turn, which is one turn longer than it needed to be
evidence: a union is checked and the error names the row, the prop and the component. A render prop resolves to nothing, so naming a value for one fails, which is right. A prop typed plainly as string takes anything, because a string has no values to enumerate
result: the boundary is in the type's own docs now. Two of the three are the technique working and the third is where it cannot reach, which a reader needs to know before trusting a green check on a row

decision: The runtime note is accurate on every count I could check
why: it is the most load-bearing document here — the vite config cites it for why this app is on Router, and the rule that no primitive is hand-rolled rests on its enumeration
evidence: the three versions it names are the three installed, its dependency list matches the manifest, and every one of the thirty-eight primitives it lists is a component subpath of the installed package. The extras in the package are esm, types and thirty-six internals, none of them components
result: a fourth survey in a row that found its subject sound. Reading a document against its source costs one command and is the only way the word accurate means anything

decision: The enumeration is pinned to the package it was read from
why: the version the note names was already checked against the lockfile, so a release adding a primitive would leave the list short while the version still read as correct — stale in the one way the existing rule cannot see
evidence: the rule reads the same place the note says it read, the package's own exports, and compares name for name and count for count. Dropping radio from the list fails it by that name
result: the note said where it got its list, which is what made it checkable. A document that names its source can be held to it; one that does not can only be believed

decision: The navigation note is accurate too, including the twelve names it rests on
why: it is the one document here I had never opened, and it describes a design for an owner this package does not have, which makes it the easiest place for a claim to go quietly wrong
evidence: the router version it pins is the version installed, its count of nine flat routes is the count there are, and all twelve affordances it names in backticks are still exported at 1.170.32 — including composeRewrites, which reads like a proposal and is a real API
result: the two count rules and the version rule already covered the first two claims. The names were the part nothing watched

decision: A design resting on twelve names is a design resting on those names existing
why: a rename upstream would leave the whole model resting on something gone, and the version pin would still read as correct, which is the same blind spot the primitive list had
evidence: the rule reads every lower camel case name the note backticks and asks the router's own declarations for it. Renaming one to useChildMatchez fails it by that name
result: only lower camel case is read, because the note also backticks the code it proposes — CanvasFrame, a FrameStack, the _splat param. Those are things it designs rather than things it found, and holding them to the package would be reading the note as a description of this app

decision: Reading grid-row was my own prescription and it cannot be done
why: I recorded a turn ago that a real raggedness check must read grid-row rather than group by geometry
evidence: an auto-placed grid child computes grid-row-start as auto, every time, so every child reports the same value and every grid reads as one row. The first attempt failed on its filters, not on using geometry
result: geometry is the only way and it needs the filters the first cut lacked: cards only, no zero-height cells. Five pages carry a grid of nothing but cards and not one row in them differs by more than two pixels

decision: The reduced-motion block is not unmeasurable, and I said it was for most of a day
why: I could not emulate the media query, and I turned that into not built rather than asking what I could read
evidence: the browser parses the block whether or not it matches. Read out of the built sheet: three named animations stopped, animations clamped to one iteration of a millisecond, and transitions narrowed to colour, background, border, shadow and opacity at the detail duration
result: movement removed and colour kept legible, which is a better contract than killing everything. What I could not do was watch it apply; what I could do was read what would apply, and those are different sentences

decision: Narrowing the property list is half the block, and the half nothing checked
why: the existing rule pinned which properties still transition and which must not, and said nothing about how long any of them takes
evidence: without the clamps a colour fades over its full length and a keyframe runs its course, so the block reads as doing its job while a reader who asked for stillness waits out every one. Replacing the duration clamp with a timing function fails the rule now
result: the built sheet resolves both clamps as the source states them, so this pins what ships rather than what is written

decision: Eight grids named a minimum a narrow screen could not hold, and two knew to guard it
why: an auto-fill track whose minimum exceeds its container overflows rather than shrinking. Two grids wrote min(360px, 100%) because 360 does not fit a phone; the other eight wrote a bare number and happened to be small enough
evidence: the guard is inert whenever the container is wide enough, so there is no threshold to argue about and no reason for two idioms. All ten read min(…, 100%) now. Measured at 375 before and after: every grid keeps its column count and its width to the pixel, on all nine pages
result: at 260 the guarded grids hold and the pages that overflowed stop, which is what the bare numbers were quietly relying on not being tested

decision: Two toolbars sat in a row that could not wrap
why: stress at 260 found the layout page still overflowing after the grids were guarded: the vertical rail was pushed to 372 in a 260 window because the row beside it never wraps
evidence: the page's rail is a flex row and now wraps. The vertical toolbar stacks under the horizontal one when there is no room and sits beside it when there is — checked at 1280, both at the same top with no overflow
result: the fix belongs to the page and not the component. A toolbar is a tray of controls and does not wrap, which is what a toolbar is

decision: A six button toolbar is 298 wide and a 260 window cannot hold it
why: after the wrap the layout page still overflows by 58 at 260, and the whole of that is the horizontal toolbar itself
evidence: 260 is narrower than any phone sold — the smallest is 320 — and every page holds at 375 and above with nothing over the edge. Wrapping the tray would break the arrow keys that walk one line of it
result: so it is recorded rather than papered over. The honest limit of a tray that does not wrap is the width of what it holds, and a consumer giving one six buttons on a phone has to give it fewer or let it scroll

decision: I said the pages were clean at 320 and that was true of one thing only
why: the document does not scroll at 320, so I called it clean and moved on
evidence: the toolbar is content sized at 298 and starts at twenty, so its right edge is 318 whatever the window is. At 320 it clears the edge by two pixels while already standing eighteen outside its own column, which the page's padding absorbs. It spills the column below 338 and the window below 318
result: no document scroll is not the same sentence as fits, and I used the first to mean the second. The number that matters for a column is the column's width, not the window's

decision: I made the grids uniform and wrote nothing to keep them so
why: the previous commit changed ten class strings by hand and left the convention resting on my having done it, which is the state the two guarded grids were already in before today
evidence: the rule reads every auto-fill track in the components and the pages and asks whether its minimum folds. Putting the foundations swatches back to a bare 128px fails it by file and by number
result: a fix that depends on nobody undoing it is half a fix. The stylesheet check already proved the new form compiles; this keeps the form

decision: The three suites I had never opened are the ones that make the class sweeps mean anything
why: render, arithmetic and utilities were unread, and a suite that tests nothing is the worst kind of green
evidence: utilities builds the stylesheet and asks whether every class the kit and the pages can emit compiles to a rule, which is why the class sweeps kept coming back clean — and it had already proved this turn's ten new arbitrary values compile. Arithmetic feeds every chart the shapes where a division reaches the markup as NaN. Render draws every export and pins that the only silent ones are the roots that wait to be opened
result: none of the three is vacuous. The one thing they left was mine to write, and it was the convention I had just created by hand

decision: Mounting the viewport did not change what a closed dialog draws, and a rule already said so
why: I changed the dialog's structure this session and wanted to know whether the list of five components that draw nothing until opened was still right by luck
evidence: it is not a skip list. The rule asserts the silent set equals those five exactly, so a dialog that started drawing markup would drop out and fail it. The list beside it that does skip work has its own rule, whose note records a name having sat in it dead
result: a hand-written set that is asserted as an equality is not the same risk as one that is consulted to excuse work. Both are here and both are guarded, which is why neither needed me

decision: Two bar charts stated their figures nowhere a reader could hear them
why: the breakdown fix generalises: a chart with an explicit label gets only that label, and bars draw no text at all, so whatever the name leaves out is gone
evidence: six bar charts on the page. Four have a readout beside them stating the latest — four thousand one hundred and eighty two, five hundred and ten — and one is a level meter where naming sixteen floats would be noise. The two release charts said releases, a floor under an empty week, and no number at all
result: both names now end with the readings, built from the kit's own barsLabel, and read as releases a week, with a floor: 8 readings, latest 9

decision: The two remaining label helpers reach the entry, for the reason the first one did
why: breakdownLabel was exported because the documentation told a consumer to call it. barsLabel and sparklineLabel do the same job for the same reason and were not exported
evidence: three components take a label that replaces a computed default, and a consumer replacing one could not reproduce or extend what they replaced. Using barsLabel on the page is what made the gap concrete rather than tidy
result: the eight helpers still unexported are internals — points, cells, shares, a swipe outcome — and a consumer has no call for them. What is exported is what a component's own documentation names

decision: The level meter is decoration because it marks nothing, and the page says so in data
why: I had excused it in a commit message and nowhere else, which is the third thing this session I called decoration on my own word
evidence: emphasis reads none there, and none is what stops the last bar taking a data-newest attribute. Counted in the page: six bar charts, and it is the only one where no bar carries that mark. The other five mark exactly one
result: the reason was already half written in barsLabel's own docs — the newest value is the one the emphasis marks, so it is the one worth naming. What the page shows is that sentence being true

decision: The default name promised a latest that the chart refused to mark
why: following that sentence to its end found the contradiction: barsLabel names the last reading whatever the emphasis is, and emphasis none paints no bar differently from the other fifteen
evidence: a consumer writing bars with emphasis none and no label of their own got a name pointing at a value the plot draws exactly like the rest. Reachable by anyone, and not by these pages, because the level meter passes a label
result: barsLabel takes the emphasis now and counts without naming when nothing is marked. The pages are untouched: levels keeps its own name, which is a fair name for something ambient

decision: The sparkline carried the same contradiction, found by looking rather than waiting
why: the bars fix named a shape — a name that points at a value the plot does not distinguish — and the sparkline has the same shape one component over, with head none hiding the dot, the glow, the drop and the badge
evidence: sparklineLabel named a latest whatever the head was. A consumer drawing a trace with no head got a name pointing at a reading the line runs through like every other. No page passes head, so this was reachable by a consumer and by nobody here
result: the head is resolved once now and decides both what is drawn and whether a latest is worth naming. All five names on the page are identical to before

decision: Resolving that value once broke a rule that was reading for the old syntax
why: the rule that asks whether a table prints a value no page draws excuses keys a component works out for itself, and it found them by matching head: head ?? at the call
evidence: hoisting to a name and passing that hid the key from it, and its own control caught the drop on the next run — the assertion that sparkline's computed set is exactly head
result: the detector follows the one hop now rather than the refactor being undone. A rule that reads syntax goes stale when the syntax improves, and the fix is to teach it the better shape, not to keep writing the worse one

decision: The grid does drop history, and I almost called the pane's artifact a defect
why: the page claims narrowing shows fewer weeks rather than smaller cells, and its label states the span it drew. At 375 the grid was still drawing 182 cells in a 293 wide box
evidence: on a fresh load at that width it draws 119 and 105 — seventeen weeks and fifteen — and each name reports what was drawn. The stale 182 was the resize observer not firing while the pane is hidden, which my own notes already warn about
result: twice now the hidden pane has produced a number that looks like a defect. The reload is the check that separates them, and it is cheaper than the argument

decision: The Start finding rests on a structural fact and the fact has not moved
why: I deferred re-testing it every turn as too large, which was true and also an excuse for never looking at what it rests on
evidence: vite in this workspace is an alias for a different product, the override reaches every package, and the peer check that would object is silenced. All three are still exactly as the note quotes them. The finding is not a version bug that could quietly age out
result: re-running it means installing Start and standing up a shell, which is the owner's call. Noticing that its ground has moved costs one read

decision: So the ground is pinned rather than the conclusion
why: the note quotes the workspace file, and the vite config cites the note for why this app is on Router. Nothing tied the quote to the file, so the alias could change and the finding would read as current
evidence: the rule reads the block the note quotes and asks the workspace for each line of it. Changing the quoted version to 0.3.0 fails it by the line
result: the peer rule is written inline in the note and across two lines in the file, so that one is read rather than matched. A quote that cannot be matched literally is still worth checking, just not with the same tool

decision: The grid's unfitted first pass is never seen, so there is nothing for a skeleton to hide
why: it measures its own box, so the first pass has no width and asks for every week it was offered. That is 182 cells where 119 fit, and a flash of the wrong grid would be worth fixing
evidence: the correction rides in the same commit as the mount. A mutation watcher, told after the work settles and before anything can be drawn, was told once for a freshly mounted pair and read 124 and 110 — the fitted counts, never 182 and 126. Both plots were new nodes, so it was not reading the old ones
result: a paint can only land at a task boundary, which is later still. Withholding the plot until it is measured would trade a flash nobody sees for a blank nobody asked for, so it is left alone. Timers are clamped while the pane is hidden, so the sampler that polls is worthless there and the checkpoint is what carries this

decision: The tray takes a second row rather than spill the column it sits in
why: it is a row of fixed-size controls, so its width is the sum of them and nothing in it gives. At 320 the six buttons came to 298 inside a 280 column, 18 past its right edge, clearing the window by two — luck rather than layout
evidence: one class. At 320 it now ends exactly on its column at two rows with every group whole, and at 1280 it is 298 by 38 with the class or without, so it is inert wherever there is room. Dropping it fails the rule by name, and wrapping a group fails it too
result: shrinking the buttons was the other option and is the wrong one: the control size is an input and never a result, the same trade the grid makes with its cells. Base UI's root offers disabled, orientation and loopFocus and nothing for overflow, so this was CSS to solve rather than a part to adopt

decision: The plot drew one column more than it had measured room for
why: the fit counts whole weeks, and the window then pads its front so every column starts on a Sunday. That pad needs a column to sit in. Both functions were right read alone, and the seam between them was not, which is why the suite was green over it
evidence: at 320 the plot box was 204 and the grid drew 217 across, so its last cells sat outside the card. A remount changed nothing, which is what separated this from the stale observer. Counting the window back from the last day makes the opening a Sunday, so no pad is needed and 14 columns become 13 — 0 past the box at 320, still 26 at 1280
result: the last column is the week in progress now, which is what this kind of plot shows anyway. The pad is left for a series too short to fill the window, where it still costs a column and the window has the room. Restoring the old body fails the new rule by the number: 11 cells asked into 7, and 7 columns into room for 6

decision: Nine pages hold their columns at 320, and the two shapes still flagged are meant
why: the tray and the plot were each found by hand on one page, which says nothing about the rest. A page that does not scroll sideways is not a page whose parts sit in their boxes — the tray ended 18 past its column while clearing the window by two, and no page-level check would have seen it
evidence: every element's right edge against the content box of the nearest ancestor that has one, skipping whatever an ancestor clips. Forcing the tray back to one line flags it at exactly 18 and the fix clears it, so the instrument reads what I read by hand. Its first form was worthless — it called a 132 wide element 300 past its parent because the parent was display contents with no box
result: the nav strip bleeds 8 by a negative margin so its edges line up with the column, and the shut icon tile's label is 9 of padding with its text clipped to nothing. Neither puts ink outside anything. Nothing else is left on any page

decision: No focus mark in the kit is clipped, and the one that would have been is now checked
why: a ring is drawn outside the border box, so a part that fills a parent which clips can be reached by keyboard with nothing to show for it. The rule that asks whether a part draws for the keyboard cannot tell a mark that shows from one that does not, so an outside ring there passes it
evidence: every focusable part against the padding box its clipping parent really clips at. My first pass measured to the content box and reported fourteen shapes over five pages, every one of them wrong: a card's own 20px of padding is exactly where the ring goes, and it is five times what a ring needs. Corrected, nine pages give one hit, and that is the detector reading inset-ring-2 as an outside ring
result: the scroll area already solves it and said so in a comment that nothing checked. Swapping it back to an outside ring leaves all 283 other tests green, so a comment was the whole protection. It is a rule now, written for the one part it is true of rather than asked of everything

decision: A card sat in a column narrower than the grid's own stated minimum
why: the widgets ask to span two columns from a window width, and the grid they span is not the window. At 640 the page column is 358, where one 200 track fits, so a span of two invented an implicit second track sized by what was left rather than by the minimum
evidence: the template read 200px 146px where two 1fr were asked for, and setting every span to one collapsed it to a single 358. The card that landed in the 146 held a shortcut whose keys and label need 128, so its label sat 20 outside the card. Only a span-one child is ever hurt: the span-two children get the full width either way
result: the span asks the container now, so nothing asks for a track that is not there. At 640 one track of 358 and the shortcut fits; at 1280 four of 211 with thirteen spanning two, which is the layout unchanged. Fixing the grid fixed the shortcut — I had the wrap ready for the shortcut itself, which would have been the symptom

decision: Sweeping one width proves one width
why: the tray and the plot were both found at 320, and I wrote down that nine pages hold their columns without saying at what width. A page is at its worst where a multi-column layout is narrowest, which is just above a breakpoint and not at the bottom
evidence: at 640 the sweep found the shortcut that 320 could not, because at 320 the layout is one column and the grid never makes the short track. 640 and 768 are clean now, 320 is clean, and the only thing left at any of them is a 3px slider track whose scroll width rounds a pixel over its client width
result: a rule now reads the pages for a span keyed to the window, so the shape cannot come back quietly. Reverting one of the six fails it by file and class

decision: The slider's leftover is its thumb, not a rounding pixel
why: I wrote in the row above that the last thing the sweep leaves is a track whose scroll width rounds a pixel over its client width. It is 3 against 8, which is not rounding, and I had not looked before writing it down
evidence: the track is the vertical rail, 3 wide and 120 tall, and the thumb it carries is wider than it is. The rail's own right edge sits 6 inside its parent, so nothing leaves the slider
result: a thumb wider than its rail is what a slider looks like. All three shapes the sweep flags are deliberate now — the nav bleed, the shut tile's label, and this — and at 320, 500, 640, 768 and 1024 there is nothing else on any of the nine pages

decision: Nothing on any page clips its own text, and the one that clips on purpose says the value
why: a card clips by default, so content that outgrows one is lost with no way to scroll to it. The horizontal sweep says nothing about that, and a fixed height is asserted rather than worked out, which is the same shape as the span keyed to the window
evidence: every element that clips its own vertical overflow, naming the text it cuts. Squashing a card to 40 reports it by the sentence it loses and clears when restored, so the sweep can see one. At 320x720, 375 and 640x460 it reports 22 and every one is a mechanism: the ticker's digit column, sr-only text, and the hidden inputs Base UI files under a control
result: the ticker keeps ten digits in the DOM and shows one by clipping, so I read what it says rather than what it draws: seven of its eight children are aria-hidden and the eighth carries the value, so a reader is told 9,562 and not the column. Composed into a readout it answers to text-readout rather than number-ticker, since the later data-slot wins

decision: A signature written on one line settled nothing the default rule could read
why: the rule that asks whether a stated default is the real one reads the destructure by line, so a component written as one line settles nothing it can see. Breakdown is that shape, and its showLegend was documented and unchecked while the rule reported it agreed
evidence: delimiting by the destructure rather than the line takes it from 25 of the 58 stated defaults to 28. Changing showLegend to false now fails it by name, and before this it did not
result: I wrote a second rule for this before finding the first, and the first is better: it resolves a named constant, so DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS reads as the 1 · 3 · 6 · 10 a page prints, which mine had skipped as unweighable. Mine was deleted rather than kept beside it. Look for the owner first — I have written that down before

decision: Base UI writes its defaults down, and the note saying it does not is wrong
why: the rule's own comment says a Base UI default is not written here and cannot be checked against, so thirty of the fifty-eight stated defaults are unread on that basis
evidence: its types carry @default: ToolbarRoot says horizontal for orientation and true for loopFocus, and the popover's trigger, root and portal each carry several. The positioner carries none, but the kit's own wrapper settles side, sideOffset, align and alignOffset itself, so those are already weighed
result: the thirty left are loopFocus, modal, keepMounted, closeOnClick, defaultOpen, disabled and their kind. Reading them means mapping a kit part to the Base UI part it renders, which is the work, not the extraction

decision: The primitive's defaults are read now, and the mapping was already written down
why: thirty of the fifty-eight defaults a page states are Base UI's, and the rule skipped them on a note saying they could not be checked. A page can say a menu loops focus by default and be wrong about it with nothing to catch that
evidence: the kit declares what it wraps: export type MenuProps = MenuPrimitive.Root.Props names the part, and a composed type names each part it draws from, so the menu's content reads its popup and its positioner together. Base UI writes @default in the interface for that part. Coverage goes from 28 to 52 of 58
result: the kit's own signature is laid over the primitive's, because a wrapper that settles sideOffset itself is what a page sees. Saying the accordion opens many by default passes all 285 against the old source and fails by name against this one, which is the whole of what was added

decision: The six left over were the reader's shape, not defaults out of reach
why: I left six unweighed and called them beyond reach without naming them, which is the assumption I had just spent the turn deleting. Naming them took one run
evidence: three were the reader: the field writes an interface that extends its primitive rather than a type alias, and the accordion's panel has an empty body that takes hiddenUntilFound and keepMounted through Pick of its root, which is where the @default sits. Following both takes 52 to 55 of 58
result: the last three are accounted for rather than skipped: two sizes come from buttonVariants defaultVariants and the union rule weighs them, and the bars' max is prose for a default worked out from the data. The rule names them now instead of counting, so a new one out of reach fails rather than lowering a total quietly

decision: Two tables printed their default as though it were one of the alternatives
why: a row's values are the alternatives and its fallback is the default, and fifteen of the seventeen rows were written that way. The tabs' orientation listed horizontal in both and the tooltip's cursor axis listed none in both, so each read as one more choice than the prop has
evidence: the tabs row rendered horizontal horizontal vertical and now renders horizontal vertical; the tooltip's rendered none none x y both and now renders none x y both. Restoring either fails the rule by name
result: I found this measuring something else — the union check printed the stated set sorted, and a repeat is visible there in a way it is not in the source. A rule that prints what it read is worth more than one that only says yes

decision: Five of the seventeen stated unions are weighed, and the short one is named
why: nothing tied a row's values to the union the prop actually takes. The rule above weighs four of them against buttonVariants, and the note said the other thirteen describe a Base UI type and could not be weighed
evidence: Base UI names fifteen closed unions across its types and no two share a name with different members, so a prop typed Side or TabsRoot.Orientation resolves on its last segment without following an import. Four resolve that way and one is a union this kit writes itself. Emptying the toolbar's orientation values fails by name
result: the tooltip's side is the one deliberate short list: Base UI also takes inline-start and inline-end, which follow the writing direction, and the table names the four a reader can picture. It is named in the rule so the omission is a decision. The twelve left are a tv variant or a prop the positioner takes from a shared interface rather than declaring

decision: The dialog's table left out the one modal value that turns modality off
why: the popover lists true, trap-focus and false; the dialog listed trap-focus and its default only, and its note named neither false nor what it does. A reader could not tell a dialog can be non-modal at all
evidence: Base UI types both the same way, boolean or trap-focus, so once the popover's positioner resolved the dialog's row was the one that disagreed. The rule found it rather than me: it failed on the row before I had looked at it
result: the row lists false now and the note says what it does. This is the second thing this pass found by widening a reader rather than by reading pages — the first was a default printed twice

decision: A part's props need not live under it, so the index is by name
why: the tooltip's side resolved and the popover's did not, which is the asymmetry that named the shape. The tooltip redeclares side to give it its own default; the popover takes side and align from UseAnchorPositioningSharedParameters, which sits in utils, outside the folder the reader walked
evidence: indexing every interface by name and following what it inherits — Pick keeps, Omit drops, a bare name brings everything — takes 5 of the 17 stated unions to 13. The four left are tv variants the rule above owns, so the remainder is complete rather than merely small
result: the body is counted by braces now, not matched to a line: PopoverPositionerProps closes as an empty pair on the line it opens, and the old pattern ran past it into the next declaration and captured the wrong body. It had worked for defaults only because that path read the inherits clause and never the body

decision: I fixed the dialog's row and left the same hole in the popover's note
why: the dialog's modal note named true and trap-focus and not false, which is how its row came to omit false too. I corrected the row and the note there and did not look at the popover, whose note had the identical hole and whose row was already complete
evidence: two rows in the whole set have a note that names its own values, and both are modal. Checking them named the popover's immediately. A fix applied to one of a matched pair and not the other is half a fix, and I have written that down before
result: both notes say what all three values do now. The rule counts from two: naming one value is a note singling out the interesting case, naming two has started a list, and a reader takes the one left out as unsupported rather than undescribed

decision: The accent is not colour alone, so the defect I went looking for is not there
why: I read both tables and saw the default separated from the other values by one class, and called it a use-of-colour failure before measuring it
evidence: the accent is 0.68 against 0.221 in relative luminance, which is 2.69 to 1 in greyscale. A reader who cannot separate mint from grey still reads it as the lighter one. There is no 1.4.1 defect and the design is right as drawn
result: measure the colour before naming the rule it breaks. That is the second hypothesis this session that a number killed, and both times the number took one call

decision: Neither table said in words which value you get by writing nothing
why: the accent carries to a reader who sees it and to one who sees only lightness, and to nobody else. The variants table is the worse of the two: its default sits among the others rather than ahead of them, so a reader was given sm md lg with nothing saying which they would get
evidence: a clipped word after the value in both tables. Nothing moves — the mark measures 1 by 1 and the visible value is still 34 wide — and the row now reads soft by default rather than soft. A render test pins it: dropping the mark from either table fails by the markup
result: the props table and the variants table are a matched pair and I did both in one go, which is the thing I got wrong on the modal note one turn earlier

decision: The deck's fallback for a refused pointer capture does what it says
why: the card catches a failed setPointerCapture, warns, and drags from state instead. Nothing had ever run that path, and a recovery nobody has exercised is a recovery nobody knows the shape of
evidence: with setPointerCapture throwing and hasPointerCapture answering false, the top card still drags the full 60 — the same distance as the control with capture working — and the warning fires exactly once. The suite server-renders only, so this is a browser observation and not a durable one
result: the deck was already sound on the rest of it: role group, a name, tabindex on the top card only, arrow keys named in aria-keyshortcuts, and every buried card aria-hidden. I went looking for a gesture-only control and did not find one

decision: A card that would not spring back was the hidden pane again, and I chased it furthest
why: released under the commit distance the card stayed where it was dragged, through a reload and past a second of waiting, which reads exactly like a state bug in the release branch
evidence: the inline style said translateX(0px) while the computed transform said 60. React had reset it; the transition to the reset value could not run. document.hidden is true, rAF ticks zero in 300ms, and six transitions were sitting there unable to advance
result: the discriminator was already written down — read the inline style the component wrote, not the computed value the compositor owes — and so was this exact case, a dragged card whose computed transform outlived a state reset. I re-derived a note I already had instead of reading it first. The commit path looked fine in the same run only because it changes text rather than animating

decision: The readme said the tables' values can still drift, and this week they cannot
why: its last line drew the line at names: a renamed prop fails typechecking, and the values were on their own. Four turns of rules moved that line and nothing moved the sentence, so the front door understated what the package does
evidence: the counts around it are pinned and were right — forty-six modules, thirty-nine with slots, nine routes — so only the sentence had gone stale. A stated default is now read from the signature or from the primitive's @default, following what a part inherits, and a stated union from the type the prop really has
result: one row escapes everything: the bars' max is prose for a default worked out from the data. The readme names it and a rule ties the sentence to the computed remainder, so saying every row is covered fails by the missing phrase. A document that understates is as wrong as one that overstates, and it is the harder one to notice

decision: The widget note is accurate, quotes included, and was already pinned
why: it is the one document I had not read and it is load-bearing: it argues from counted evidence and quotes the code it argues about. A note whose quotes have drifted is worse than no note, because it reads as authority
evidence: all ten composites it names are exported, the POC it counts is at the path it gives, and every one of the seven text roles it quotes is byte-identical to text.tsx. The readme's badge and terminal blocks match too — seventeen quoted strings, none wrong
result: its counts were pinned already and so were its quotes, by a rule that reads each block's file comment and compares against that file. The note also corrects itself in place where the owner overruled its scope rule, which is why it has not gone stale

decision: I wrote a duplicate rule for the second time today, and the same way
why: I measured that quoted class strings could drift, confirmed they had not, and wrote a rule. An existing rule failed on the same mutation, which is the only reason I found it. Earlier today the same thing happened with the stated defaults
evidence: both incumbents are stronger than what I wrote. This one reads the file comment on each quoted block and compares against that file; mine asked only whether a string appeared in any component, so a badge class quoted as a terminal's would have passed it
result: the miss is the same both times: I searched the data for a gap and never searched the suite for an owner. One grep for the subject noun — quote, default — finds it. The lesson as written, look for the owner first, did not stick; the version that might is grep the suite before writing the rule

decision: One unusable reading took the whole sparkline, not its own place in it
why: the bars filter a reading that is not a number out of their ceiling and give it the floor, and the breakdown counts its share as nothing. The sparkline did neither, and its arithmetic spread the fault rather than containing it: NaN in the extent makes the span NaN, NaN is falsy so the || 1 guard hid it, and every other point came back NaN. An SVG path of NaN draws nothing at all
evidence: its own test claimed to cover series that would break naive arithmetic and listed empty, single, flat, huge and signed — every case but the one that breaks it. Reverting the filter fails the two new tests by name
result: the reading sits at the low now, which is where the bars put one. Found by asking which components have a guard and which do not: two of the three readouts had nine NaN assertions each and the third had none of the case that matters. A sibling that hardens is the standard the other two are measured against

decision: The grid told a reader its total was NaN, and spoiled four lengths besides
why: the sparkline fix generalises: a reading that is not a number reaches the DOM as words or as geometry. As words it is honest, and a ticker handed NaN printing NaN is right. In an attribute it is neither — the browser drops the declaration and nothing reports it
evidence: a sweep over every component that takes a number, reading attributes only and stripping text. Bars, breakdown, ticker and the mended sparkline are clean. The grid leaked twice: one count that is not a number was the whole of the total in its aria-label, which is all a reader who cannot see the plot is given, and an unusable cellSize spoiled a row height, a month offset, seven line heights and the column width
result: the count is summed only when it is finite and the size falls back to its default, which is what the bars do with a ceiling. Extracting that default to a constant broke the rule that reads stated defaults from the signature, so the rule now resolves a scalar constant as well as an array one

decision: The sweep passed its own mutation, because one guard hid the next
why: written as a single hostile row per component, the grid's unusable weeks emptied the plot, so the summary summed nothing and the count fault had nothing left to spoil. Reverting the count guard passed all 292
evidence: one case per fault. Split into four rows for the grid, reverting the count guard fails by the aria-label it writes. The read-first assertion is the summary itself now, so a fixture that stops reaching it fails rather than going quiet
result: I nearly recorded a guard as proven on a run that could not see it. The mutation is the only reason I know which of the two it was testing

decision: Two components named themselves with words they had not been given
why: the same question as the numbers, asked of text. A barcode builds its bars by repeating its value, so an empty one draws nothing and was announced as order followed by a space. An avatar with a blank name carried aria-label of the empty string, and one of spaces carried four of them
evidence: an element named with nothing is still exposed, and a name of whitespace is worse than none: it overrides the initials underneath rather than letting them stand. Measured before deciding — 0 bars and order-space, and aria-label equal to empty and to three spaces
result: the barcode says no order, which is the voice the kit already uses for no readings and nothing left. The avatar drops the attribute instead, because its name is the consumer's to give and there is nothing to fall back on, and the initials then name the tile. Both fail by name when reverted

decision: Two assertions in one test, and the first hid the second
why: reverting both fixes at once failed on the barcode and stopped there, so the avatar half was unproven on that run. The same shape as the hostile row that hid a second fault one commit earlier
evidence: reverting the avatar alone fails on its own assertion, so both halves are covered. A test with several assertions proves only as far as its first failure, and a mutation that trips an early one says nothing about the rest
result: mutate one thing at a time even when the fix is one idea applied twice

decision: Six more components let a blank label override the name they give themselves
why: ?? catches a label nobody passed and not a label made of nothing, so an empty string reached the attribute and won. Every readout that names itself from its data had it, and so did the grid and the deck, whose defaults are plain words the destructure only applies to undefined
evidence: the avatar and the barcode were the first two found by hand, and the general form was one grep of aria-label across the components. A sparkline given an empty label announced nothing rather than 2 readings, latest 2
result: the two whose default is a word now keep it in a constant, so the signature and the fallback read from one source and the rule that checks stated defaults still resolves it — which is why that rule learned scalar constants an hour earlier. Each of the six was mutated on its own rather than together, because the shared test stops at its first failure

decision: Two cards on the widgets page answered to one name
why: the kit says on three separate label props that two of a thing on a page need two names, and nothing checked it. Both breakdowns there drew the same data under language split, TypeScript 84 percent, WGSL 9 percent, CSS 7 percent, so a reader met the name twice with nothing to tell the cards apart
evidence: what distinguishes them is the legend, which is aria-hidden by design and so reaches nobody. Naming the second for what it hides is the only difference a reader can be given. One duplicate across nine pages, so the rule reads clean
result: a page's labels are read as written rather than as rendered: two identical expressions are two identical names whatever they interpolate. Binding was the case I set out to check and is not one — no keys renders an empty span and the action, which names nothing falsely. No name and a name naming nothing are different faults

decision: Every id a page points at is an id a page has
why: a name given by reference fails silently and completely: a dangling aria-labelledby leaves the control with no name at all, and nothing about the markup looks wrong. The kit leans on Base UI to wire these, so the question is whether the library keeps its side
evidence: 51 references across labelledby, describedby and controls, on the three routes that have form controls; the other six pages have none, which is right for pages with no controls. None dangle. Pointing one at a name nothing carries is seen and clears when restored, so the zero is not a blind one
result: it cannot be a suite test, and the reason was already written down beside the slider: Base UI registers the label's id after mount, so server markup carries no aria-labelledby at all. That note had driven six tracks on one page; this is every reference on every page

decision: A blank name on the slider cannot be typed away, so it is not worth the machinery
why: its union takes a label or an aria-label and a consumer can satisfy either with an empty string. Unlike the six labels mended this morning there is nothing to fall back on: a slider has no data to name itself from
evidence: a generic parameter would reject a literal empty string and would not reject a computed one, which is the case that actually happens. Dropping the attribute when blank changes nothing either — a control with an empty name and a control with no name are both unnamed
result: so it stays as written, and the limit is recorded rather than papered over. The type says a name is required and cannot say the name means anything, which is where a type stops

decision: The references that only exist while something is open resolve as well
why: the closed sweep found 51 and none dangling, but the ones most likely to dangle are the ones a closed page does not have. A popup names itself by pointing at a title that mounts with it
evidence: driven open one at a time: a popover, a menu of four items, a dialog, and a combobox filtered to five. Every reference resolves — the dialog carries both a labelledby and a describedby, the menu's content and its group each point at a title, and the combobox's controls points at the list it opened
result: the combobox needed the documented path rather than a click: arm focus with an inert key press, focus from JS, then type a real character. A click alone left it closed, which is the note's own warning about synthetic events on a controlled field

decision: Aria-activedescendant cannot be observed here, and the run that looked said nothing
why: after typing to open the combobox, ArrowDown set no activedescendant and highlighted nothing, which reads exactly like a component that does not use it
evidence: a listener on the document proves the key never arrived: nothing at all was recorded for the press. Only character input reaches this page, which my own note already said — the new part is what it costs, that this attribute is out of reach here entirely
result: so the combobox is unmeasured on that point rather than clean on it. I nearly wrote down that it sets no activedescendant, which would have been a claim about the browser tool wearing the component's name

decision: The select opens onto a real listbox, and the hidden input the note promises is there
why: its trigger is a combobox role with a listbox popup, so what it opens and what it submits are two different elements and either could be wrong on its own
evidence: open it draws one listbox of four items with aria-selected on svg, which is the word the trigger shows. 36 references on the page and none dangling. The hidden input that carries the value is a sibling of the trigger inside the field, with no name because the demo passes none, which is right
result: I read no input inside the select first and nearly doubted the note that promised one. There is no data-slot=select element at all, so closest() never matched — the filter was wrong, not the claim. Check the instrument before the document

decision: The manifest says only CSS has a side effect, and nothing checks that it is true
why: a rule pins the declaration to exactly one entry, which keeps it from being edited by accident and says nothing about whether it is honest. A module with a top-level effect makes it a lie that costs a consumer its tree shaking silently
evidence: no shipped module has a bare call statement or touches a global at module scope — 48 scanned. What is left unproven is subtler: every component calls tv at module scope, and a bundler that cannot prove that call pure keeps it, so importing one component may evaluate all 46
result: proving that needs a real bundle rather than a read, and the package is private with one consumer in this repo, so the harness costs more than the answer is worth today. Named rather than built
